en.goal: Greet someone, say goodbye and say thank you in a basic interaction.

lines: I'm doing well, thanks! And you?

bonjour-vs-bonsoir.title: "Bonjour" or "Bonsoir"?
bonjour-vs-bonsoir.body: We use bonjour from morning until late afternoon — it's the standard greeting of the day. In the evening, when arriving somewhere, we switch to bonsoir. Salut, on the other hand, works at any time of day, but only with friends or people you're close to — never with strangers or in formal settings.

svp-informal.title: "S'il vous plaît" in everyday life
svp-informal.body: In casual speech or text messages, s'il vous plaît almost always gets shorter: with friends it becomes s'il te plaît (the "tu" form — the informal "you" — not "vous", the polite or plural "you"), and in writing you'll often see just STP. The full "vous" form is still the safest choice with strangers.

a-bientot-informal.title: Among friends, "à bientôt" becomes "à plus"
a-bientot-informal.body: With friends, à bientôt is common, but in everyday speech (and almost always in text messages) the most common goodbye is à plus — and in writing it usually becomes just A+. With strangers or in formal settings, "à bientôt" is still the right choice.

la-bise-cumprimento.title: Why do French people greet each other with kisses on the cheek?
la-bise-cumprimento.body: Besides saying "bonjour", it's very common to greet friends and family with la bise — one or more light kisses on the cheek (the number varies by region: 2 is the most common, but in some regions it's 3 or even 4!). With strangers or in formal/professional settings, people shake hands instead.
examples: to greet with a kiss (or kisses) on the cheek

trueFalse.claim: This is what we say when someone helps us a lot.
trueFalse.whyNote: Correct — merci beaucoup means "thank you very much"; it's exactly what you say to thank someone for their help.
